title: Wind Tunnels: More Important Than You Realize
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant open with banter about bad breath, masks, and flossing, then turn to wind tunnels. They cover how the hosts' own indoor skydiving commercial relates to vertical wind tunnels, and how most research tunnels use scaled-down models whose data is corrected with math. The episode traces early flight history: Benjamin Robbins' whirling arm, George Cayley's work on lift and drag and his glider, Frank Wenham's 1871 tunnel, and the Wright brothers' own tunnel in Dayton, Ohio. It then explains how a modern tunnel works (settling chamber, contraction cone, test section, diffuser, drive section), open versus closed circuit designs, and fans placed behind the model. Other topics include sting and balance force measurement, boundary layers, flow visualization with smoke and oil, supersonic and hypersonic tunnels, NASA Ames' large tunnel, NASCAR and Formula One tunnels, the Virginia Tech anechoic wind tunnel for wind turbine noise, and whether computational fluid dynamics will replace tunnels. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about the Wetlands club in New York.

segments.title: Opening banter and wind tunnel introduction
segments.summary: The hosts joke about bad breath from masks and flossing, then introduce wind tunnels and their interstitial shorts and a Toyota commercial shot in an indoor skydiving facility.

segments.title: Types of wind tunnels and scale models
segments.summary: The hosts explain vertical and horizontal wind tunnels, use of desktop scale models with math used to correct data, and the link between wind tunnels and aerodynamics and aviation.

segments.title: Early flight and Benjamin Robbins' whirling arm
segments.summary: Early human flight attempts focused on flapping like birds. Benjamin Robbins used a whirling arm in 1746 and found drag and shape mattered more than flapping. Lift and drag became central ideas.

segments.title: George Cayley and early gliders
segments.summary: George Cayley used his own whirling arm and identified lift as key. He built a glider flown by a coachman and later was credited with an early flying machine. The hosts mention a monk, Elmer of Malmesbury, with an early recorded flight around 1010 CE, and note that the Wright brothers are credited with engine-powered flight.

segments.title: Frank Wenham and the first wind tunnel
segments.summary: Frank Wenham of the Aeronautical Society of Great Britain built the first wind tunnel in 1871, twelve feet long with a steam-powered fan. The airflow was still choppy.

segments.title: Wright brothers' wind tunnel
segments.summary: The Wright brothers built their own wind tunnel in Dayton, Ohio, tested many wing shapes, and finished tests by 1901. Their first powered flight came in 1903. Early tunnels had turbulent air, which led to smoother designs.

segments.title: Anatomy of a modern wind tunnel
segments.summary: A modern tunnel has a settling chamber, contraction cone, test section, diffuser, and drive section. Open and closed circuit designs are described. The fan sits behind the model so air is pulled over it, which is smoother than pushing air.

segments.title: Measurement, boundary layers, and flow visualization
segments.summary: Models are held by stings and balances that convert forces into electrical signals. Boundary layers, viscosity, and compressibility affect results. Tunnels can simulate humidity, temperature, pressure, and icing. Smoke, oil, and high-speed cameras show airflow. Supersonic and hypersonic tunnels use compressed air bursts.

segments.title: Modern wind tunnel uses and future
segments.summary: Examples include NASA Ames' very large tunnel, Formula One and NASCAR tunnels, and a Virginia Tech anechoic tunnel with a Kevlar wall for testing wind turbine noise. The hosts discuss whether computational fluid dynamics will replace tunnels and conclude tunnels are still needed.

segments.title: Listener mail: Wetlands club
segments.summary: Brian from Queens writes about the Wetlands Preserve nightclub in Tribeca, open 1989 to 2001, which hosted musicians and ran an environmental activism center.
